title: Opinion: SPACs, the backdoor IPO, are making a comeback. But should they?
html:
J. Ari Pandes is an associate professor of finance and an associate dean at the University of Calgary’s Haskayne School of Business. He is also a research fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute.

Just when we thought the obituary had been written on special purpose acquisition companies, or SPACs, the numbers show they are clearly alive and well in the U.S. In 2025, the U.S. saw 144 of these companies – which have no operations and raise money solely to merge with a private company – go public, compared to 90 traditional initial public offerings.

This year, through October, there have been 158 SPAC IPOs already. While this is far from the pandemic-era boom of 613 SPACs going public in 2021, I think it’s safe to call it a comeback. SPACs boomed during the pandemic, when near-zero interest rates and a hot market for speculative growth stocks had investors chasing the next big thing. The SPAC market collapsed in 2022 as interest rates rose and post-merger share prices tumbled.

For those unfamiliar with how SPACs work, here’s a quick refresher. A sponsor, who can be an individual or a deal team, puts up some initial cash and then sets up a shell company, which is listed on the stock exchange through an IPO.

The IPO investors pay US$10 a unit, which typically includes a common share and a fraction of a warrant. The warrant allows the holder to buy a share at a fixed price, usually US$11.50, for up to five years after the merger. The money sits in a trust, earning interest while the sponsor hunts for a private company to merge with. When the merger closes, the private company becomes public.

Sponsors put up the initial cash, typically a few million dollars, by buying warrants. That money covers the upfront underwriting fee and the costs of finding a private company to merge with. They also get founder shares that are equal to 20 per cent of the SPAC for about US$25,000.

This stake only has value if a deal is completed, so the incentives are razor-focused on finding a deal, otherwise the SPAC is liquidated and the sponsor loses its initial investment. And since an SPAC typically has 18 to 24 months to find a deal, the clock is ticking, which can push a sponsor toward a bad deal rather than no deal.

Jay Ritter, a University of Florida economist and leading authority on capital markets, compiled statistics on SPAC mergers completed from 2012 to 2023. The analysis found that for investors who bought shares in the newly merged companies at the close of their first day of trading, the equal-weighted three-year buy-and-hold return averaged -57.7 per cent. Over the same period, the average buy-and-hold market return was 17 per cent, so that investors earned a dismal market-adjusted return of -74.7 per cent. The 2015 cohort was the only one out of the 12 during that span where these investors subsequently beat the market.

The early evidence from the 2024 and 2025 cohorts suggests that the dismal post-merger performance is continuing. By comparison, companies that went public through a traditional IPO over the same period earned an average three-year return of 8.2 per cent, or −25.1 per cent on a market-adjusted basis.

Not great, but much better than the results from companies going public by merging with an SPAC. So why do SPACs keep getting formed with such poor post-merger returns?

It’s because some people are making a killing.

Investors who buy in the SPAC IPO get a money-back guarantee. Before the merger, they can redeem their shares for the cash in trust plus interest, if they want to, a feature known as the redemption option. But they get to keep their warrants, which pay off if the merged company does well. Essentially, investors have a default-free Treasury bill with a lottery ticket attached. Hedge funds – typically the early investors – love it.

A 2023 study by Ritter and two co-authors finds that these SPAC investors earned 23.9 per cent a year, on average, between 2010 and 2020. Sponsors did even better, earning average annualized returns of more than 100 per cent on deals completed through early 2021. So, it’s really the early investors who capture the gains, while the everyday investor buying into the post-merger company bears the costs.

But the companies going public pay a cost, too. The same research finds that between 2015 and early 2021, listing by merging with an SPAC cost the median company 15.1 per cent of its market value, which includes underwriting fees and dilution. For comparison, a traditional IPO cost 3.2 per cent.

So why would a company take this route? One likely reason is the classic lemons problem. The companies that take the SPAC route are more often unprofitable and possibly the ones that aren’t attractive to investors through the traditional IPO route. The poor long-run returns provide some merit to the argument.

Closer to home, we have also been seeing this play out. Earlier this year, Xanadu, a Canadian quantum-computing company, merged with Crane Harbor Acquisition Corp. and began trading on Nasdaq with a cross-listing on the TSX. It drew attention because it was effectively the first Canadian tech company to debut on the TSX since 2021.

This was followed by General Fusion, a B.C. fusion-energy developer that went public through an SPAC on the Nasdaq as well. Not to say that these companies are lemons, as they are long-term bets whose payoff may be years away, but it is a fact that neither has rewarded post-merger shareholders so far.

As of Nov. 20, Xanadu is down about 83 per cent from the US$10 SPAC price, and General Fusion is down about 58 per cent. On a market-adjusted basis, shares are down 92 per cent and 50 per cent, respectively.

In Canada, the SPAC market has been subdued, with only one SPAC listing on the TSX in 2025, compared to the 144 in the U.S. And not a single SPAC has listed on the TSX so far this year. SPACs never really took off here like their close relative, the Capital Pool Company program on the TSX Venture Exchange, did.

We certainly need more companies going public in Canada, but maybe our quieter SPAC market has been a good thing.
summary: Despite widespread poor post-merger returns, some people are making a killing with SPACs
